decision.detail:
I turn from the coffee cups and say to Rita and Larry, "Hey. I'm gonna walk over to the ballroom and sit at that piano. The party's tonight, right? I'm playing a set. Twenty minutes, maybe thirty. Give me the afternoon."

I don't wait for them to object. I pull my coat on, walk the two blocks to the ballroom, and sit down at the bench. The keys are cold and a little sticky. I start with something simple—"Clair de Lune," or maybe just a chord progression I half-remember from a wedding I covered in '94. My fingers fumble. I start the phrase again. The van backfired twice outside; I hear it through the glass and don't turn around. I play the same eight bars for the fourth time, slower, letting my left hand find the bass notes by feel instead of sight. I'm not good. I'm not going to be good by tonight. But I am here, at the keys, in the room where the party is, and my hands are doing something instead of my mouth saying something.

I stay at the piano. I work through the tune in pieces. I lose my place. I go back to the top. The light in the ballroom goes from white to gold. I'm still at the keys.
decision.intention:
The driver can find the jack. The Rialto will close. The coach will sit in the lot. I already took that route last Tuesday—boarded, rode, called my sister, confirmed the van, said the right words, and woke up in this bed with the radio telling me it's Tuesday again. Reaching Pittsburgh didn't do it. So I'm not boarding the coach.

My theory, untested: the loop breaks the way it breaks in the film. Not by going somewhere. By *being* here, doing the work with my hands, playing the same eight bars until they aren't the same eight bars anymore. The ending isn't a destination. It's a Tuesday where I'm at the piano and I'm not performing for a camera and I'm not selling a forecast. I'm just a man learning a tune in a ballroom that smells like old carpet and lemon polish.

If I play that set tonight, and Rita hears me, and I'm not the weatherman on the screen—then maybe Wednesday is the thing that comes after. I don't know. I haven't tested it. But it's the only act I've got that matches the ending I'm trying to reach, and it's the one I can do with my hands right now, in this room, where the keys are cold and the light is going gold.
decision.words: "Give me the afternoon. I'll be back by five. And Larry—don't let anyone book the ballroom for a corporate thing. I need that piano at eight."
